utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. All of a sudden it looks strange in a different courtroom. Yes, if the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. I hope you are feeling okay today, Mr. Garic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the volume could be put up a little bit so that I can hear the interpretation more easily, just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder if you could follow the interpreter's request. Could you turn up the volume a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This was the witness's request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Garic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D6079, please. We have the English translation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, please have a look at this document. Did you give the Defence team a statement, and is the statement on the screen in front of you in fact the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the statement on the 2nd of November, so I signed the statement on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the statement correct? Does it accurately reflect what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, I did my best to make it as accurate and reliable as possible. I drafted this statement to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put the same questions to you today, the questions contained -- would your answers be the same as those contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the substance of my answers would be the same, perhaps not word for word but the substance would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, could I tender this statement into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2379, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the documents also be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many documents are you tendering, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're tendering four documents which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they on the 65 ter list previously, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, they were but under a different number. There had been some miscommunication between our investigators and case managers and they uploaded the statements under different 1D number which was in fact on the 65 ter list. And we now switched it back so that it's the correct number, but that number doesn't appear on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So four of them are on the 65 ter list all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: They're on the 65 ter list but under a different number, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask one question about 1D10010, probably its 65 ter name is different on your list. It's a city map marked by the witness of his family home. How is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's simply put in there for background information, but if you don't believe it's relevant or an integral part of the statement then we don't have to have that received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will not admit this. In relation to other three documents, are there any objections, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So three items excluding the city map marked by the witness will be admitted into evidence. Shall we give the number right now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 1D10011 will be Exhibit D2380, 65 ter 1D10012 will be Exhibit D2381, and 65 ter 1D10035 will be Exhibit D2382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a summary of Mr. Momir Garic's testimony in English. [In English] Momir Garic completed electo-technical school and then a degree on All People's Defence at the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo. He did a shortened programme of military service in the Koprivnica Garrison of the JNA lasting for four months and 30 days. In 1985 he started working in the Territorial Defence staff in Novo Sarajevo, where he remained until March the 1st, 1992. The TO staffs commanded two types of the Territorial Defence units, area and manoeuvre units. The area units were organised by local communities and local organisations or enterprises. There were a number of big enterprises in the territory of Novo Sarajevo municipality which had numerically strong and well-armed Territorial Defence units, buying the most modern weapons and equipment in the Yugoslav market, very often even before the JNA units. During the first half of 1991 [sic] he learned about the organising of Muslim paramilitary forces. People who had no connections with the Territorial Defence started to visit its commander very often, who was -- the commander was Muslim. These people were well-known Muslim extremists and violent people that he knew from the town. In Pofalici he often saw people wearing green berets, many of which he knew to had been in conflict with the law, that is, had a criminal past. After the murder of Nikola Gardovic on March the 1st, 1992, citizens started to organise watches in their buildings, suburbs, and urban areas. This was not a nationally exclusive organising, but rather organising of citizens regardless of the ethnicity. On April the 4th, 1992, Serbian members of the MUP special units set off for their new bases in the MUP school in Vraca which they had been allocated in an agreement on the partition of the MUP, common MUP. Instead of peacefully entering the new bases, the Serbian specials were ambushed by the Muslim colleagues and two of them were killed. On the 6th of April, 1992, under the pretext of celebrating the day that Sarajevo had been liberated in World War II, the Muslim authorities organised a big public rally. Muslim snipers fired at the crowd from the surrounding tall buildings and they immediately blamed it on the Serbs. When the war started at the beginning of April 1992, the Territorial Defence staff in the Sarajevo municipalities where Serbs lived were mobilised and they took it upon themselves to defend the people from attacks by Muslim extremists, because the JNA was already falling apart and could not provide any guarantee in this respect. Since Momir Garic had previously worked in the Territorial Defence matter, he was assigned as one of the supervisors in the Territorial Defence staff which operated in the part of the Serbian part of Novo Sarajevo municipality. They organised a unit of the Territorial Defence members from the Serbian part of Novo Sarajevo municipality. It was an organised group of citizens that set up a line of defence of the Serbian suburbs that ran in front of houses, suburbs, and streets with a mainly Serbian population. There was not a single instance in which the Serbs attacked a suburb with a Muslim majority. These initial lines of separation remained at the -- the same throughout the war. During the middle of May, 1992, in order to protect the Serbian majority population of Grbavica, the JNA [sic] launched an action to move the lines on the left bank of Miljacka river and gain control of Grbavica. This was a typical combat action. Yet since Grbavica was not held by anyone the action was completed by a movement of Serbian forces with minimal use of weapons. The line established remained unchanged until the end of the war. From the beginning Muslim snipers fired at Serbian territory and a large number of members of the Serbian Territorial Defence were killed, but the number of civilian victims was particularly large. Momir Garic knows about the position of the forces ranged against them as well as in the depth of the territory and on dominant heights around the city, such as Igman, Bjelasnica, but also in the city on Hum hill, Mojmilo hill, Zlatiste, Colina Kapa, Jajce barracks, among others. Muslim armed provocations occurred on a daily basis until the beginning of May 1992. On the 2nd and 3rd May of 1992, Muslim forces launched heavy attacks on JNA units in Skenderija and Dobrovoljacka Street in which several dozen JNA members were killed, many more injured and several hundred taken prisoners. Between 4th and 6th May, 1992, the JNA's 216th Mountain Brigade arrived in Novo Sarajevo municipality with the task to safe-guarding the withdrawal of the remaining units from Sarajevo and preventing an escalation of conflict. As the brigade was short of personnel, units of the Serbian Territorial Defence from Novo Sarajevo joined its ranks, resulting in the establishment of the 3rd Battalion. Momir Garic was member of that battalion until 11th or 12th September, 1992, when he started working in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. On 16th of May, 1992, Muslim forces launched a powerful attack on Pofalici. Many civilians were killed and some of them are still missing 20 years later. According to Momir Garic the strategy and the operational goals of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was to prevent the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from breaking into the Serbian territories, which would have been fatal for the Serbian population. This breakthrough of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have had a huge effect on the development of the situation, on other fronts, and the whole course of the war in BH. His unit fired at the enemy only in defence and did not intend to cause civilian casualties or terrorise civilians. They were aware of the provisions of the international humanitarian law and respected those rules. They never received orders from a superior command or civilian authorities to attack means of public transportation. They were clearly informed of the location of military targets and kept strictly to that. He knows that Muslim forces misused civilian facilities for military purposes. The officers and men in his unit were drawn from the local population and had already learned basic military skills while serving in the JNA. There were also younger people who had no military experience. From its composition it can easily be concluded that it was a people's army which was primarily defending its own homes and was very reluctant to move away from there. The general position of the Serbian civilian and military authorities was to allow the passage of supplies of humanitarian aid to civilians in the part of the town controlled by the Muslim authorities. The Serbian forces never brought into question regular supplies of humanitarian aid, least of all with the aim of achieving any military goal. Momir Garic knows that Muslim forces misused humanitarian convoys to smuggle weapons and ammunition and that they also used the Red Cross sign to mark military vehicles and military commands. He also knows that Muslims did not allow Serbs and other inhabitants to leave the city. And I have one correction. The 216th Brigade came in Sarajevo by middle of April, not in May, beginning of the May. [Interpretation] That would be all for the moment. For the time being I have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing, in the form of a statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. And you will be now cross-examined by the Prosecution. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we commence, we think it is probably prudent to provide this witness with a caution under Rule 90(E). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I discussed with Mr. Tieger this before. If Prosecution is of the view such warning is warranted, please tell us, the Chamber, before the witness starts his evidence. Mr. Garic, before you start your -- answering the questions by the Prosecution, I wanted to let you know the specific Rule in the Tribunal which says to the effect that you may object to the -- to answering any question that might tend to incriminate you. However, in such case, the Chamber may compel you to answer such questions; but in that case, your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in subsequent proceedings against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Garic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 1D26007, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garic, in your Defence statement, the one that's just been admitted as your evidence at paragraph 28 on page 6, you explained that you had been shown the transcript of the statement you gave to the Prosecution in 2004 and you said you had no corrections to make to that transcript except for a few clerical errors that you specified in that paragraph. And we can see now the first page of that -- of the transcript of that statement you gave to the Prosecution is on the screen. So I take it from what you said in your Defence statement that with these corrections you've made you agree that the statement you gave to the Prosecution in 2004 is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 2004, but on Friday when you allowed me a little extra time I was told that he was an investigator from The Hague Tribunal, but I discovered he was from the Prosecution. He promised that he would provide me with all the recordings, the CDs, so I could see what it was about, but that was never done. And not long ago I received them and I read through this statement on that occasion from 2004. I didn't have enough time to read through it thoroughly, but in substance, yes, that is what it is. There's nothing much that should be changed or amended.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you were asked today in court the same questions you were asked when you gave that interview, would you give the Court the same answers - and not necessarily word for word but in substance the same?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, in essence, yes. Quite a long time has passed since then, eight years after all, but basically, yes, my answers would be the same. Perhaps not word for word, but the substance would not change. That's one thing. But secondly, the Defence team did not prepare a statement for me as you've said. I gave that statement. There are perhaps minor amendments that were made that don't change anything much. So this is my statement, not the Defence team's statement. And also when you mentioned the fact that the witness should be cautioned or warned, what sort of caution did you have in mind? Could you perhaps clarify this for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honours would like to clarify the -- the witness has asked about the caution. Perhaps he didn't understand fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the caution that the Prosecution referred to is the one that Judge Kwon gave you, which you said you understood. There's no separate caution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I misunderstood, Your Honours. Thank you. On the basis of the witness's answers, I'd like to tender this interview. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we would object to that. I don't think that 92 ter necessarily encompasses another party other than the party calling the witness introducing a statement wholesale. So absent any -- if there's extensive reference to the statement, maybe at some stage we could admit it, but at this stage I don't think it should just come in. I point out the text of the Rule 92 ter (A)(ii) has a condition that the witness is available for cross-examination. So I think that this was intended for use as an admission by the party calling the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before coming -- before we deal with this, Ms. Gustafson, you referred to paragraph 28 of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I said paragraph 28, page 6, because there seems to be typographical error I think when this statement was amended. So there are two paragraph 28s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we upload that first -- oh, the paragraph 28, that appears after para 33, the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's the one, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here he said: "I have been shown the transcript. I have no corrections to make to that -- to the translation of the interview." And what is your basis to object to the admission of such document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. President, it's being offered under 92 ter and it's our position that Rule 92 ter applies to the calling party and not to the cross-examining party. And in support of that, I'm calling your attention to 92 ter(A)(ii) which has as a requirement that the witness is available for cross-examination. And to me, that -- since we don't have the right to -- of cross-examination, that means that a 92 ter statement is one offered by the calling party only. And I've also pointed that if the document has value for impeachment purposes to such an extent that the admission of the entire interview seems warranted by the Chamber, at that stage it may very well be admissible, but I don't think it's admissible in the way it's being offered now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what's the point of referring to his earlier statement in your 92 ter statement at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I believe that the investigator who took that statement was under the impression that it might be an associated exhibit, but we've decided we didn't want it to be an associated exhibit and therefore we haven't offered it under -- as an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But why did you include that passage at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Again, I believe that passage was included by the investigator that took the original statement under the impression that perhaps that statement could be an associated exhibit to the 92 ter package, but we decided that it was not appropriate for a statement to be an associated exhibit because you've directed that the 92 statement be a single document, not a compilation of the witness's prior statements. So we essentially have adopted a practice here in The Hague when we see a statement taken by one of our investigators that refers to a previous statement, we don't make it an associated exhibit. And that was our reasoning for not including it as an associated exhibit although it's referred to in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think this is basically an issue of form over substance. The witness -- this is the document we have, it's available. It could certainly be tendered as a regular exhibit. The witness has agreed, however, to the steps under Rule 92 ter, so there's no reason why it shouldn't be admitted under that rule. And there is -- there are helpful details in the statement about, for example, documents that have already been admitted into evidence. I may also be relying on certain extracts from the interview depending on the witness's answers today. So it's an -- obviously an admissible document. It's relevant. It's probative. The witness has authenticated it. Call it what you will, Rule 92 ter or just under the regular Rules of admission; however, the witness has agreed to the 92 ter steps. So I don't see a problem with it going in under that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't read this -- the investigation -- how do you call it? This is a transcript of the investigation interview. I haven't read it. But I'm speaking for myself and I'm speaking sort of hypothetically. If the current 92 ter statement has been revised to such an extent that would warrant asking the witness to testify viva voce to clearly understand, it is for you to raise that issue beforehand. I hope you would have followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I don't think that -- that is not an issue here. I'm not -- I'm not relying on the interview for that purpose specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then could you specifically tell us the point of tendering this interview in more concrete terms. If necessary, we can ask the witness to be excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be a good idea or if the witness doesn't understand English he could just remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a good idea. Yes, Mr. Garic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some, but in principle I would say no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's okay. Could you kindly take off your headphones for a while while we are discussing the matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are two points basically. The first is that there is positive evidence that this witness provided in his OTP interview, including details about persons present in Prosecution documents that have been admitted, and I refer, for example, to P2583, which are Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff meeting minutes discussed at pages 47 to 52 of the interview; and another Crisis Staff document P2575, discussed at pages 29 to 40 of the interview. The other issue is that in his earlier interview with the Prosecution, he was played a number of intercepts in which he was purported to be one of the participants. I intend to use some of those intercepts as well as other intercepts we have relating to this witness, and depending on his answers today I may be relying on portions of his interview. So those are the two basic reasons for tendering the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't you tender only those parts that covers those topics?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine as well. We can -- once the witness's evidence is concluded, we can identify the relevant extracts and tender extracts from the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you object to that exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, yes, I do, Mr. President. I think that it ought to be put to the witness if there's some inconsistency between his statement and what he testifies to in court today. I don't think it should be left for later without the witness being here and given an opportunity to explain any inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness confirmed the veracity of his interview in general terms in [indiscernible]. So what's the basis of not admitting that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because if it's being used for impeachment which is what she's identified, then it's only fair to the witness, and for it to have any probative value as impeachment it has to be put to the witness, and that's a cardinal rule that we've been following in terms of the probative value of documents which are used for impeachment or to contradict the witness. The witness has to be given a chance to comment on it. So to just admit it at the end without giving the witness a chance to comment on it I don't believe is fair to the witness or to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the Chamber's position: If you read the 28th -- actually, para 34 of his statement without reading the content of the statement you cannot understand what he's saying here about. So in that case, that may be classified as, in general terms, one of the associated exhibits. But having known the Prosecution is minded to use that part of -- or, the part of the statement in order to contradict the witness's statement, it is necessary to put specific parts of the statement to the witness. However, in this -- in the future if similar situation arises, the Chamber may consider ordering the Defence to lead the witness viva voce from -- at the outset. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson. [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] I hope you understood. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Garic. I'd just like to ask you a few questions about the first meeting you had with -- or the meeting you had with the Defence in the summer of this year, where your -- you gave the Defence a statement and we were provided with a draft statement on the basis of that meeting. And I'd just like to ask you a few questions about that interview and meeting that you had with the Defence. First, how was the meeting conducted? Was your statement audio or video recorded?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I have not been receiving interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Are you hearing anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now do you hear me, Mr. Garic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I do. Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's try again, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And thank you again, Mr. Garic, for your patience. I'd like to start by asking you some questions about the meeting you had with the Defence I believe in the summer of this year. I understand that you provided the Defence with a statement and we were given a draft statement on the basis of that meeting. And I'd like to ask you whether that interview that you had with the Defence, whether it was audio or video recorded?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about what happened this year, this current year, last summer?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I did not talk with the Defence. I spoke to a man who organises witnesses who are supposed to come here to The Hague to testify. I provided my statement in east Sarajevo. We had a couple of telephone conversations and nothing was recorded. My statement was taken in writing. I read it. I made some changes. I supplemented it. Because at the moment when I provided the statement, I simply could not remember some things. So at the end of the day I wouldn't say that I changed much or anything in that statement of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a few follow-up questions from that. You said you spoke to a man who organises witnesses. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: His name is Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said: "We had a couple of telephone conversations and nothing was recorded. My statement was taken in writing. I read it." I'm still a little confused. Did you simply speak with Mr. Savcic by telephone or did you actually meet in person?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I have already told you that I met him in person once. That's when my statement was recorded, and then we spoke on a couple of occasions by phone and that was it. I saw him personally once. That's when the statement was taken, and then we had a couple of telephone contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how was that statement recorded? Was it recorded by an audio or video device?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: No. There was neither an audio or video device. I told him what I remembered. That was taken down, and that's what you have here. That's what was sent here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that in the transcript it says it was recorded, but that doesn't mean that there was audio or video involved. The witness said that the minutes of his words were taken. He did not use the word "recorded."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness said an interpret -- which was interpreted as what -- "I told him what I remembered. That was taken down ..." Now, I think that meant the same thing. Shall we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So basically, Mr. Garic, what I'm getting at is I'd just like to understand how some of the changes that we saw to your statement came about and how the erroneous information got into the draft statement based on your meeting with Mr. Savcic. And in particular, the draft we received based on your meeting with Mr. Savcic had several references to you being either a supervisor in the TO or a battalion -- and a battalion commander in the VRS. And now I understand since you've arrived in The Hague those references have been removed and you insist that you were not a commander. So did you initially tell Mr. Savcic you were a commander and then you later realised that was incorrect or was that a mistake that Mr. Savcic made in recording your statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: We had the conversation in east Sarajevo, and after that Mr. Savcic took notes based on the questions he asked me and the answers I provided to those questions. I did not correct things in The Hague because I did not get to see that written statement that Mr. Savcic sent here. When I arrived here, I reviewed those things. I said that I was involved in the organisation of defence of the Serbian people because I was professionally involved in the Assembly of Novo Sarajevo municipality in the Territorial Defence staff. And before the arrival of JNA units, before the Army of Republika Srpska was set up, there was no system of subordination in place --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, I'm going to interrupt you. I'm sorry. We'll get into the substance of your evidence in a moment. Right now my question is quite a simple one: Did you tell Mr. Savcic you were a commander or is that a mistake he made in recording your statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: He didn't even ask me whether I was a commander or not. I believe that that would -- that that was Mr. Savcic's mistake. He should not have written that down because at that time there were no appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, there were two references to you being a battalion commander in the VRS at a time when there were appointments quite clearly. So again, do you have any idea how those two references to you being a battalion commander in the VRS got into your initial draft statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I've just told you, I'll repeat. I was involved in the Territorial Defence staff as a reserve officer, a professional, and when the unrest broke out I was a member of the Territorial Defence staff --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: -- I was doing my job and I am sure that you will ask me questions about -- in other words, I didn't have --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again. I don't believe you've answered my question, but in the interests of time I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 23959, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garic, the map that's going to appear on your screen in a moment, it's a higher-resolution version, in fact, of the map that you drew for the Defence in connection with your interview. And it's referenced in paragraph 13 as 1D10035. And at paragraph 13 of your statement that's now in evidence you described your line of defence in April 1992 as stretching from the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks below Mojmilo hill and by Ozrenska Street in Vraca and the Sarajevo bypass to the Jewish cemetery and then towards Zlatiste and the road to Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in on the red line that's drawn in this map which is right around in the middle of the statement -- sorry, the map. And a little bit more and zooming in on the area where it says "Novi Grad." So a little bit to the left. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a line that you drew, Mr. Garic, your line of defence in April 1992. And the street names have changed since then in relation to this map, but your line basically goes along Ozrenska Street towards Novi Grad and it includes Mojmilo hill within your line. You see Mojmilo hill there with the number 680 approximately in the middle of the map?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: But the Serbian people did not defend itself on Mojmilo but below the Mojmilo hill, at its foot towards Lukavica. On Mojmilo there were paramilitary Muslim forces that already in 1991, or, towards the end of 1991 held their positions there. So the Serbian guards that had been organised by the Serbian people were at the foot of Mojmilo, not on Mojmilo. That's how I would put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the Chamber has heard evidence - and I would refer to Van Lynden's evidence at T2414 - that the Bosnian Serbs initially at the early stages of the war held Mojmilo hill and it was taken by the Bosnian Muslim forces sometime not long after that. So the line you've drawn here is consistent with evidence this Chamber has received, at least in relation to this time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at D572 now. And if I could tender this map as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be invited to explain his previous claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your last comment was not put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually moving -- I'm on the same topic. I'm move to a document. I'll continue discussing this very issue with the witness in relation to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But -- and you said you're tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not admitted as one of the Defence exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It was not listed on the revised 92 ter notification that we received on Friday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe it's the fourth document that was admitted --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in any event I'd like to tender it anyway because the one that the Defence uploaded is basically illegible because it's not sufficiently -- there isn't sufficient resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me check.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and it was my mistake --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be heard on something, I have a proposal to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be asked to specify the temporal aspect of the map because it is indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- through that both Mojmilo and the waterworks were held by the JNA at one point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm cutting you here. It is a subject you may take up in your re-examination. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in connection with the comments that Mr. Karadzic has just made if we could look now at D572 which is an SRK report from the 26th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, there was water-supply system on Mojmilo hill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a water-supply system on Mojmilo hill; right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So if we could look at the second paragraph of point 1 in this SRK report from the 26th of May, 1992, it says: "The composition of armoured mechanised units located at Mojmilo water-supply system is under sniper fire and two soldiers have been wounded. The enemy attacks on daily basis in a very organised manner in the wider region ...," et cetera. This document from the SRK command indicates indeed that Mojmilo hill was held by the VRS at this time, and this is the 26th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand why Rogatica is mentioned here. It says the general Rogatica sector. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That follows the comments about the armoured mechanised units on Mojmilo water-supply system coming under sniper fire. Doesn't appear to be relevant to that. The statement that the armoured mechanised units located at Mojmilo water-supply system is under sniper fire, that statement indicates that at this time the VRS controlled Mojmilo hill and, in fact, had position there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But this is in the area of a different municipality. I think it's the water-supply system that belongs to the Novi Grad municipality and the unit of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But that's a different unit that has nothing to do with the territorial units that were deployed in the vicinity of Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Garic, this is a later period of time when the SRK was formed. The point is simply that the Bosnian Serbs held Mojmilo hill, as indicated on this document, on 26th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes. The VRS was established on the 12th of May, but I'm talking about the Territorial Defence. As far as the Territorial Defence is concerned, they were in the direction of Vraca to the right of this unit. But that was on the right flank. I never went to that part of the territory, but I can claim with full responsibility and with certainty that the members of the Territorial Defence who were on that line were under the Mojmilo hill, beneath the Mojmilo hill, and not at the water-supply system at Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to another topic, which is the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. Now, when you were interviewed by the Prosecution in 2004, you were asked: "Did you attend any meetings of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff?" And you answered: "I was present at a few meetings in Lukavica, Pilava, Vraca only. I was present at only a few meetings." And that's at page 26. So I'd like to ask you what specific locations in Lukavica, Pilava, and Vraca you attended Crisis Staff meetings, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, I have understood your question. I attended Crisis Staff meetings in the headquarters of the municipality where I worked. And now I can claim that I wasn't at such a meeting in Lukavica. I was later informed of things, but I wasn't there at the time. The date referred to is the 29th of January, and on that date it was impossible for me to attend that meeting because I was celebrating the day of St. Sava and a few days prior to that day I'd take a few days off and a few days off after that date --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: -- so I could not have attended that meeting on the 29th. That's out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think, in fact, you're anticipating a question that I didn't, in fact, ask. My question was simply: Based on your statement to the Prosecution that you were present at a few Crisis Staff meetings in Lukavica, Pilava, and Vraca, where those meetings were -- took place. And your answer was: "I attended Crisis Staff meetings in the headquarters of the municipality where I worked, and now I can claim that I wasn't at such a meeting in Lukavica." So is your evidence that you never attended any Crisis Staff meetings in Lukavica, contrary to what you told the OTP in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't tell the Prosecution, or rather, the investigator that I was in Lukavica. I said I wasn't there. I was in the headquarters of the Municipal Assembly of Novo Sarajevo where I worked and I was in Vraca in a local commune in Vraca and in Grbavica in the local commune Bane Surbat, but not in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 1D26007, page 26, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I know you probably can't follow this in English, but I'm going to read it out to you, Mr. Garic. The first full question on the page where it says "JTH," the question is: "Did you attend any meetings of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff?" And your answer is: "I was present at a few meetings in Lukavica, Pilava, Vraca. Only ... I was present at only a few meetings." And then the investigator goes on to ask you who was in charge. So I'd like to ask you again: Is it your evidence today that you did not attend any Crisis Staff meetings in Lukavica, contrary to what you told the investigators in 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I suggest that we show this interview in the Serbian language too. This will help us to remind the witness of what he was asked about and what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We don't have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the witness does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The passage was read out to the witness. I take it that the witness understood the question. Mr. Garic, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood quite a bit. Here I can see that Lukavica is referred to. Pilava, it's not Pilava -- Tilava, Vraca. I said I was in Vraca in the Municipal Assembly of Novo Sarajevo. As for Pilava and Lukavica, I don't remember having said that to the Prosecutor or the investigator. I don't remember having attended those meetings. I was in the headquarters of the Municipal Assembly of Novo Sarajevo where I worked. I was in the local commune of Vraca. I was in the local commune as far as I can remember of Pante [phoen], Bane Surbat at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So your evidence is you don't remember what is recorded in this transcript of your audio-recorded interview and you weren't at any Crisis Staff meetings in Lukavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: That is my position. That's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go now to P2583, and this is a part of the transcript that I would be relying on but perhaps it's better to wait until the end of the witness's evidence before dealing with the admission of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garic, I think this is the meeting about which you anticipated I would ask questions because it was shown to you in 2004. And from your earlier answers I understood this is what you were talking about. It's the minutes of a Crisis Staff meeting held in the Lukavica local community on 29 January 1992. And it says the meeting is attended by and there are -- is a list of names including yours, and it indicates that two people are absent, Dragan Sojic and Milenko Jovanovic. Now, I believe you also confirmed to the Prosecution in 2004 that you knew all the people who in attendance -- listed as being in attendance at this meeting and they all knew you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I know all these people and they know me too. Bogdanovic, Radomir worked in the Municipal Assembly of Novo Sarajevo. Vucetic, Dragan worked in the Municipal Assembly of Sarajevo. Nastic, Nebojsa worked in the Assembly. Sarovic, Mirko, Sarovic, Mirko. Gajovic, Dobro, he didn't work in the Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly, as far as I can remember. He worked in some European insurance company. Neskovic, Radomir, as far as I can remember, didn't work in the Municipal Assembly of Novo Sarajevo. He worked for the television. And then there's myself. Kovac, Drago, yes, he worked in the Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly. Jugovic, Ranko, the headquarters of the Serbian Democratic Party, the municipal committee was in the municipal building so he was there. Djurovic, Zarko, yes, he worked in the Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly. And Prijic, Milivoje didn't work in the Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly. As far as I can remember he was the director of Galenika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Garic, Momo is your first name, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Momo. My name is Momir Garic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the name here, Momo Garic, in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Momir Garic, and I'm telling you again that at this meeting of the Crisis Staff held on the 29th, I'm telling you again that I did not attend this meeting. As I have already said, the date is the 29th of January. I gave you the reasons. I wasn't at the meeting because I was celebrating on that date. I can't leave guests at my home in order to attend a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But a few minutes ago, Mr. Garic, you said that was your name. It's transcript page 29, line 15. I'll read out the part of the transcript. "Neskovic, Radomir, as far as I can remember, didn't work in the Municipal Assembly of Novo Sarajevo. He worked for the television. And then there's myself." You said Momo Garic was yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What you read from the screen was "Momo Garic." You told us that that was you, and now you're saying it's not you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm just looking at the date of the meeting and of those who attended the meeting. Momo isn't the same as Momir. It's Momir, not Momo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Whether or not you attended this meeting, can you show the witness para number 10 of this document, probably next page for the B/C/S. I apologise, Ms. Gustafson, if I pre-empt you. But number 10 says: "All battalion commanders to be called to the Crisis Staff meeting. In charge: Momo Garic." Whether or not you attended this meeting, does this refer to you, Mr. Garic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the date of the document is the 29th of January, 19 -- the 29th of January. I don't know which commanders are concerned, the battalion commanders. I'm telling you that from the very beginning of the war there were no battalion commanders. The only legitimate military forces were the JNA and the police. While I worked in the Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly, this concerned the reserve and military composition of the Territorial Defence before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, Momo is a nickname and one of the names that it is a nickname for is Momir; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Momir is the name, and the nickname that is used is Momo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for reference, this document is discussed at pages 47 to 52 of the interview. Now, I'd like to move on to talk about the activities of the Novo Sarajevo TO that you discuss in your statement. And at paragraph 12 of your statement you said when the war started at the beginning of April 1992 the TO staffs in the Sarajevo municipalities where Serbs lived were mobilised. And you explain that in your municipality: "... we organised a unit of TO members from the Serbian part of Novo Sarajevo municipality." And that's at paragraph 13. Now, my first question is not based specifically on the statement, but it's this: Other than you, did this Serb TO unit that you formed include any other members of the former Novo Sarajevo TO who were ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: If you could repeat your question I would be grateful. I didn't understand the last couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. The question is about the Serb TO unit that was formed in your municipality. Other than you, did the unit -- the TO unit that you formed include any other members of the former Novo Sarajevo TO?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence staff of Novo Sarajevo was of mixed composition. It included various ethnicities, there was Serbs, Croats, and Muslims in it so its composition was mixed. When situation became complicated and when it was said that some sort of misfortune would happen -- the Serbian side isn't guilty, as far as I'm concerned. On that occasion the Serbian people started organising themselves and there was certain advisors who advised them as to where they should set up defences for their houses so that paramilitary formations didn't enter the territory and slaughter their families and destroy their property. Apart from me who was a Serb in the Territorial Defence staff, there were other Serbs who also had an advisory function. But it was only in the area inhabited by Serbian people, Tilava, Lukavica, Vraca, Gornji Kovacici, Miljevici, Petrovici, in these areas inhabited by Serbs alone. And whenever there were conversations about establishing such guards --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you again. I'd like you to focus on the specific question that I ask and limit yourself to answering that specific question. I understand that there were other Serbs from the former multi-ethnic TO staff that also had this advisory function that you referred to. What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander was a Muslim. He worked with me in the staff --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, you've misunderstood my question. You explained that the former -- that the multi-ethnic Novo Sarajevo TO that you were an employee of before the war included other Serbs. And then I believe you explained that those other Serbs also had an advisory function in the new Serb TO that was established in your area. My question is: What were the names of those other Serbs from the former multi-ethnic TO staff who had this advisory function?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, there was Serbs who worked with me in the staff of the Territorial Defence up until the beginning of the war. There was Ilija Kovadarica [phoen], Jovo Tadic. Those are the Serbs who worked in the Territorial Defence staff. I was a Serb. And maybe there were one or two others whose names I cannot remember, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There was a secretariat for National Defence as well from the Novo Sarajevo Municipal Assembly and it was also of mixed composition. That was in the Secretariat for National Defence. There was Serbs, Croats, and Muslims too in the secretariat. The scope of the activities of the secretariat and the national -- and the TO overlap. The Secretariat for National Defence had records on all members, had information about them, and the Territorial Defence staff was involved in training the units that were part of the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were a reserve officer with the rank of captain at this time; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And were there any other members of this Serb TO unit that you formed in April 1992 who were ranking officers, either active or reserve?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Do you have in mind people who worked with me on a professional basis in the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking about this unit of TO members from the Serbian part of Novo Sarajevo municipality that you formed in April. In that unit, were there any other ranking officers, either active or reserve?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no active officers. There were professionals but no active officers. There were reserve officers, as many as you like. There really were a lot of reserve officers, officers, and junior officers because Novo Sarajevo municipality covers an extensive territory and had a lot of inhabitants. This is the area of Tilava, Lukavica, Vraca, Kovacici. There were a lot of reserve officers, officers and junior officers as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember any of the names of the officers? Forget about the junior officers for now, but any of the officers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I remember the ones who were in the Territorial Defence stamp -- staff and they were recorded -- they were on record in the secretariat and the staff was involved in training with such units. I do remember quite a few names of people who were in the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you list the names that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remember certain names of certain individuals, but there were quite a few reserve officers, junior officers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was asking just about officers. How many?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you an exact number. Believe me, I would need some time to think about it and remember. It covered fairly extensive stretch of territory: Tilava, Lukavica, Vraca, Kovacici, Petrovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained that already. Roughly how many officers, not junior officers, officers were in your Serb TO in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand your question to mean how many officers, not junior officers, how many officers there were in the Territorial Defence from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I couldn't provide you with a number but there were quite a few reserve officers, quite a few reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said in your statement - this is a statement that's been admitted as your evidence - that there was no commander of this Serb TO but that: "As an experienced officer of the TO Novo Sarajevo and a reserve officer, I engaged in helping people to organise positions and protect them from the Muslim paramilitary forces." And that's at paragraph 12. So is it fair to say from your evidence that within your unit you were one of the more respected members in light of your position as an experienced TO member and a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In the area I lived up until the time the war broke out, the honest people was -- respected me. And so in Lukavica, Tilava, and Vraca, in that area when just before the war it was announced that there would be a difficult time for the Serbian people. We organised guards there, neighbours, friends and so on --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: -- were involved. There was no quarrelling and no disobedience --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, if you could just please answer my specific questions. Your evidence, including all of this detail about the activities of your unit, is in your statement and that's in evidence for the Court to consider. I'd just like you to answer my questions now. And the next one is: In this period in early April 1992, did your TO unit have any kind of headquarters or base or any similar type of location where they would gather?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, they would gather in local communes, Tilava, Lukavica, local commune Vraca, local commune, they would gather in houses, and so on and so forth. They would gather in local communes, discuss matters, problems, the various dangers, threats that we were exposed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Was the Pajaco facility in Vraca one of those locations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the locations. It was in the immediate vicinity right across the road from the police station. The police building. There was a police academy there before the war and when the war started it was the police that was located there. So it was in the immediate vicinity. There's only a road that separates it from the police. And Pajaco is in fact a house that was abandoned, and it was used by the members of the Serbian Territorial Defence and by volunteer as they would assemble there to discuss matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That would be a good time to break if Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at three past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, I'd like to move on to a different topic now, which is the arrival of the 216th Mountain Brigade to Novo Sarajevo. And at paragraph 22 of your statement you said the brigade arrived in mid-April. The Chamber has heard evidence from the chief of operations and training for the 216th Brigade. He testified for the Defence. His name was Stevan Veljovic. And he testified that the 216th Brigade arrived in Sarajevo on May 3rd, 1992, and that's at transcript page 29234. And, in fact, your draft statement that we received said that the brigade arrived between the 4th and 6th of May and you've now changed that to the middle of April. Is it possible that you're mistaken about the date of the arrival of the 216th Brigade and in fact it arrived somewhat later than you've said in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my first statement I stated that they arrived at the beginning of May, maybe on the 2nd or on the 3rd. Later on, on reflection, I realised that they arrived either in mid- or the second part of April, although in my first statement I did state that that brigade arrived at the beginning of May. On reflection, I now believe that they arrived somewhat later, which is why I altered that part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And what caused you to change your mind about the date of arrival of the brigade between this past summer and when you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that I had a long and hard thought about that, and after that I realised that they arrived in April, either in mid-April or the second part of April. It was on reflection. I pondered over what I remembered and I now believe that they arrived in April, either in mid-April or in the second part of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll ask my earlier question again. Is it possible that the chief of operations and training of the 216th Brigade, Stevan Veljovic, is correct that the brigade arrived around May 3rd and that you are mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: It is quite likely. It is quite possible that he knows the exact date. I believed he also had an order pursuant to which they arrived. So I believe that he is right. I myself also stated that originally; however, as I reflected on the whole situation after a long and hard thought I arrived at the conclusion that they arrived in mid-April. I don't know what Mr. Veljovic's rank was, but I do believe that they had received an order specifying the date when they should be dispatched, hence he probably knows when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you explained that when that unit arrived, members of the Serbian TO from Lukavica, Tilava, Miljevici, Petrovici, and part of Gornji Kovacici were formed into a battalion. That's at paragraph 22 of your statement. And you explained that you were not the commander of that battalion. Who was appointed battalion commander when your TO unit joined the 216th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: All able-bodied men, military conscripts, that is, were merged with that brigade; i.e., that brigade absorbed the entire staff into that professional military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in your statement you said that the Serbian TO from these villages were formed into a battalion. Who was the commander of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I have already stated that there were no appointments of the command cadre at the time. People like I was and other reserve officers who enjoyed prominent reputation in their villages were selected. There were no formal appointments. Only when that unit arrived did they introduce a system of subordination and all the staff was absorbed in that unit. Everybody was given an establishment position in keeping with their capabilities, ranks, and other relevant elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And that's exactly what I'm asking you about. When that unit, the 216th Brigade, arrived and the -- your TO was formed into a JNA battalion - which you said you think was the 4th Battalion - who became the commander of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be provided with his statement where it says the 3rd Battalion in paragraph 22. That's what you can read in paragraph 22, the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the end of the 22nd paragraph. That's what I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, where there's a reference to the 4th Battalion. Do you want me to repeat my question, Mr. Garic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: No, no. I understand your question perfectly well, and again I'm saying that everybody, all able-bodied men, were absorbed by that unit. They became its members. And as far as I can remember, the commander of that battalion when it became part of the professional army was the reserve officer Brane Palackovic, I remember that I remember his name correctly, Palackovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your position in the battalion once it was incorporated into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Before I joined the Ministry of Defence in mid-September, I did not have an establishment post. I spent a lot of time travelling from Lukavica to Pale and then to Jahorina. That's where the seat of the government of Republika Srpska was. I was involved in talks there leading to my transfer to the same job I did before the war in the Ministry of Defence because the remit of the Ministry of Defence and the staff of the Territorial Defence where I worked before the beginning of the war, before April 1992, are similar. I had the necessary qualification and that's why I spent more time at Pale and on Jahorina looking for a place where I will be employed permanently, where we'll -- where I will gain a livelihood.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. What -- you said a moment ago that the -- that when that unit - referring to the 216th Brigade - arrived, they introduced a system of subordination and all the staff was absorbed in that unit. Everybody was given an establishment position in keeping with their capabilities, ranks, and other relevant elements. I understood from that answer that your entire TO unit was incorporated into the 216th Brigade. Are you saying now that you actually didn't become part of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, I repeat that until the arrival of the professional army, there were no appointments. There were people who advised the Serbian population, and then I spent the entire period, lasting for two or three months, travelling from Lukavica and Pale to Jahorina looking for a job. I wanted to do exactly the same thing I did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Garic. Let me ask it this way: Is it your position that you were never a member of the 216th Brigade of the JNA or the VRS once the 216th Brigade was transformed into a VRS unit in May?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I was a member of that unit. I was a member of that unit, but I did not have an establishment post. I was never appointed to an establishment post.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you keep your rank as captain?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I had that rank before and when I joined the Ministry of Defence pursuant to the laws governing the work of the armed forces and the Ministry of Defence, I was promoted by two ranks in the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: -- I don't know how long --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry, I think we're straying away from the topic. When you became a member of the 216th Brigade, did you keep your rank as captain?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I was a reserve captain and that -- I kept that rank until the moment I joined the Ministry of Defence. In the Ministry of Defence, I was promoted first to the rank of major and then lieutenant-colonel, so I kept that rank, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So notwithstanding your rank as a captain within your battalion within the JNA structure, you had no -- what you've referred to as establishment post. So I understand from that you were just a regular member of that battalion. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I did not have an appointment. I was not a foot soldier either. I moved around. I moved around the sector. I would go to the command of that brigade, but, I repeat, they gave me a lot more free time in order to talk about my new job and I spent more time travelling between Lukavica and Pale and Jahorina than in the place where the military was, where their command post was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you're unable to specify what your position was within the 4th Battalion of the 216th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I don't know if we're talking about the 3rd or the 4th Battalion, I can't remember. In any case, originally it was the Territorial Defence but later it merged with the brigade. As far as I can remember, I did not have an appointment in that brigade. I'm sure that I didn't until the moment I was transferred to the Ministry of Defence when I was given a permanent position which at that time was known as work obligation. It was my permanent work position but it was called work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the commander of the 216th Brigade at the time was Dragomir Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I believe that the commander was a lieutenant-colonel and that his name was Dragomir Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to go back in time and look at the activities of your TO unit before - at least how I understand it - before it was incorporated into the JNA. And I'd like to start by playing an intercepted conversation from 21 April 1992, which is P5703. So if you could just listen to this conversation and then I will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] "It is the Serbian municipality village. "What's up? "How are you Momo? "How can you assist us with manpower. "As soon as possible in manpower? "Yes. "Wait till I check out. "Do you have any armoured -- "Yeah. "We sent one. "When? "This morning. "Well nothing, just a few. Just a few. "They're coming from all sides. The army won't use tanks. Nothing. "They won't even move the tanks. "No, no, by God, do you have anything? "The number? "621-116. "Just calling and we'll push it a bit. "621-106. "Aha. "And if you gather those and send them to Vraca, please. "Okay. Old man. "Bye then."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Garic, in this conversation a person who is identified -- who identifies himself as Momo and who is identified by the intercept operator as Momo Garic calls a certain Velibor in Ilidza asking for assistance with manpower. Velibor tells him to call Prstojevic. Then Momo asked Velibor to sent men to Vraca. And I think you explained earlier that Vraca was in your area and, in fact, it was -- there was a location in Vraca where your TO would gather. So this is, in fact, you asking for manpower to be sent to Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: In 2004 I stated in Belgrade that I do not remember this conversation. I'm really not clear. I really don't understand. I don't remember this conversation. I do not remember ever having communicated with Ilidza and asking for something. Believe me, despite my great wish to help the Court and you and everybody else, I really do not remember this conversation. I do not remember ever having conducted this type of a conversation, getting in touch with Ilidza. I really don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you said you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest -- because if I leave this for my additional examination, it hasn't entered the transcript that one of the collocutors said that the military did not want to move anything, they didn't want to move the tanks or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army was not helping and that's why somebody is asking a favour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When the witness says he doesn't remember this. There is no point of putting that question to the witness. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honours, this is an exhibit, it's in evidence, the transcript is available.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said you don't remember having this conversation. Do you remember -- do you know Nedjeljko Prstojevic, or did you know him at the time, the commander of the Ilidza Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedjeljko Prstojevic, I know him superficially just by sight. I don't think I ever communicated with him. I know that he lived and worked in Ilidza. We did not have any contacts. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to play another intercepted conversation from the same day, 21 April 1992, and this is Exhibit D1202. If you could again listen to this conversation and then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting I would like to say that I did not have any objections to anything. I just wanted to correct the transcript. We heard something, but that did not make it to the transcript. I wanted to make a correction on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the collocutors said the army doesn't want to move the tanks, they don't want to do anything, and he expresses his despair for not being able to defend his people, whereas the army did not want to help. That did not make it to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean that that part of the conversation was not reflected in the exhibit itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think the problem seems to be that Dr. Karadzic has heard something that's not reflected in the transcript of the conversation. He's not referring to the transcript of our LiveNote. So perhaps we could ask that this be referred back to the language section and they could check the exhibit to see if it accurately -- is translated accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just note for the record that the passage the accused refers to is in the transcript of this intercept, P5703, so it's in evidence, regardless of what ended up on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garic, let's listen to this conversation from the 21st of April, 1992. This is D1202.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unidentified male person: Yes? "Momo Garic: Good afternoon. "Unidentified male person: Good afternoon. "Momo Garic: May I speak to Danilo? "Unidentified male person: Danilo? "Momo Garic: Yes. "Unidentified male person: Danilo who? "Momo Garic: Veselinovic. "Unidentified male person: Well, you've got the wrong number, my son. Where are you calling from? "Momo Garic: And is Mr. Prstojevic there? "Unidentified male person: Who are you and where are you calling from? "Momo Garic: I'm calling from Novo Sarajevo" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we break for five minutes? There's some technical difficulty with my headphones. We'll rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we begin with the intercept again?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, that's Exhibit D1202.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Unidentified male speaker: Yes? "Momo Garic: Good afternoon. "Unidentified male speaker: Good afternoon. "Momo Garic: May I speak to Danilo? "Unidentified male speaker: Danilo? "Momo Garic: Yes. "Unidentified male speaker: Danilo who? "Momo Garic: Veselinovic. "Unidentified male speaker: Well you've got the wrong number, my son. Where are you calling from? "Momo Garic: And is Prstojevic there? "Unidentified male speaker: Who are you and where are you calling from? "Momo Garic: I'm calling from Novo Sarajevo.
