utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to play one last portion of this intercept which is the very end and it starts at 14 minutes and 17 seconds and goes until the conclusion of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Neso Garic: I didn't want to ... "Momo Garic: Yeah right, that's better. "Neso Garic: That's it. "Pass on my regards to Momo. If I'm able to, we'll see each other, God willing. I might stay for two-three days. "Do they have any money? "Well, our people. Do any of them have anything? "Momo Garic: To be honest, I have no clue. "Neso Garic: Are you lot getting anything? "Momo Garic: Well, there are from friends and relatives ... "Neso Garic: Right, Momo. Have a nice day. "Momo Garic: Give my best to everybody over there."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garic, we've heard much of this conversation in which two individuals who identify each other as Neso Garic and Momo Garic, and you've explained that you had a -- or you have a relative named Nenad Garic and you said perhaps his nickname is Neso. The two discuss what was then the recent attack on Pofalici and the effect the attack has had on their relatives and acquaintances, and this is something that you've discussed at length in your Defence statement and also in your OTP interview in 2004. And in particular, the Momo Garic in this intercept states that his kum was slaughtered in the attack. And in your OTP interview, you said that you heard rumours that your kum "Krsteni [phoen]" which was translated into English as godfather was slaughtered in the attack on Pofalici and that's on page 16 of that interview. And the Momo Garic in this intercept explains that following this attack on Pofalici his parents are somewhere in Pale. And in your OTP statement in 2004 you stated that after the attack on Pofalici your parents stayed briefly in Lukavica with you and then they went to stay in Praca with some relatives, that was at pages 16 and 17 of the interview. And Praca is a village in Pale municipality. And in light of all those coincidences, it's quite clear, is it not, that this is you speaking with Neso Garic; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Nenad Garic is, indeed, my relative. Again, I cannot recognise my own voice. I can't recognise it. However, the facts do prove the golgotha of everything that happened to the Serbs in Pofalici. That was the first ethnic cleansing. I am saying that I cannot recognise the voice, but I can talk to you about the golgotha of the Serbian people in Pofalici about the slaughtering and about the terrible, terrible fate of the Serbian people. My parents stayed until the 16th. I stated they didn't stay until the 16th, but I now claim that they did stay until the 16th and my wife and my two children and myself left before the beginning of the civil war because my son had been wounded in a car accident. The place that I resided is hilly and that's why we moved to Lukavica, where we stayed with my wife's parents. I repeat once again that my parents stayed in Pofalici where we had resided, and I'm talking about Donji Pofalici with a mixed composition of the population consisting of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. On the 15th, on the eve of the attack --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but there is extensive detail about the attack itself in your evidence. My question is more about the identity of the speakers. And I take it you don't dispute that all of these facts about you - your name is Momo Garic, you were -- your friends and relatives were affected by the attack on Pofalici, your kum was slaughtered in the attack, and that your parents ended up moving near Pale after the attack - you don't dispute both of those things are true, both of you and about the Momo Garic speaking in this intercept, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Everything was as you have just stated. I have explained all that in my statement at great length and I can go on talking about that at great length, but again I cannot recognise my voice and I also cannot say that that was my relative Nenad. Whether I spoke to him or not, I don't remember. But this is just a segment of that golgotha, of that misery of all that -- those terrible things that happened in Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you don't dispute that any of those facts are true; you just have no recollection of any conversation you had with Nenad Garic after the attack on Pofalici about that attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that we spoke at that time. I believe that the telephone lines did not function at that time. This is not my voice. This is not Nenad's voice either. And as for the details, the details are all correct. However, everything is distorted. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at some of the things that you and Nenad - or it's my position that it was you and Nenad speaking in this intercept - said. And I'd like to go to the transcript of the intercept and in the first part I'd like to have you look at is at page 15 of the English and the B/C/S. Sorry, my mistake, if we could go to page 6 of the English and the B/C/S. I apologise. And it's at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and about the middle of the page in the English. And this is where Neso says: "That part, are you lot holding anything?" And Momir says: "Well, this, it's holding up." And Neso says: "Well, will it be possible to keep hold of that, of the left part, at least?" And Momir says: "Yes, sure, of course." And if we go to the next page in the B/C/S Neso says: "It will?" And Momir responds: "Yup." And Neso says: "Well, hold on to it then damn-it, only what needs doing is that we at bash up what we don't need on the left side." And if we could go to the next page in the English, Momir says: "Yup, right, that's the thing." Now, this is a reference to the Bosnian Serb forces keeping control of the left bank of the Miljacka and bashing up the parts of the left bank they do not control by shelling those parts; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the word "polupa [phoen]" "bash" means. If you think that this refers to shelling, it was impossible to shell anything down there because there were Serbs living there, not only there were Serbs, but I also believe that artillery was never used against civilians irrespective of what their ethnicity was or what their religious affiliation was. As far as I know, fire was opened only on the observed military targets which were confirmed. In the inner city of Sarajevo where I was, there were dozens, if not hundreds, of such targets. But shelling an urban part of the city where the civilian population resided, I claim again and again that that was never done, not even celebratory fire was opened. But when a military target was observed, when it was confirmed and double confirmed, then yes indeed fire was opened at such targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify your last answer, is it your position that -- you said: "By shelling an urban part of the city where the civilian population resided, I claim again and again that that was never done." Is it your position that urban parts of the city where the civilian population resided were never shelled?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I am saying that if it was confirmed with certainty that there was only civilian population there, then such areas were never targeted. But there were hundreds of military targets, mobile targets, command posts, groups from which fire was opened, but fire was never opened on urban neighbourhoods where the civilian population resided or at least that didn't happen while I was there up to mid-1992, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the reason why fire was never opened on urban neighbourhoods where the civilian population resided, is that because of the risk that such shelling would cause to the safety and lives of the civilians in those neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that would be that more or less. Because that would mean innocent casualties, the loss of life of innocent, honest victims and it never occurred to anybody to do that, either military or civilian. But there were individuals. But at the time when I was there, there were few of such individuals who had infantry weapons. They were somewhat excitable, but they could not get hold of any heavy weaponry. The army as an organisation, as a command, at that time up to mid-1992 never did that. They only fired on observed targets which were military targets, and this is understood when I say "observed targets" which were confirmed and there were hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to page 20 of the English and page 21 of the B/C/S. And this is at the -- in the bottom third of the English page and the top of the B/C/S page. And here Neso asks, and this is starting at the second line of the page: "Uh-huh, Ilidza's holding up well, right?" And Momir responds: "Well, it is, it is." And Neso asks: "And is Hrasnica ours?" And Momir responds: "Well, I don't know. It's been pretty flattened so ..." And Neso asks: "And down there, or Sokolovic Kolonija." And Momir responds: "Oh fuck it, Neso, I don't know. It's been pretty damaged as well. They're now saying that our people have gone in down there tanks, to clear out our apartments. What do I know? " And Neso responds: "Right, right." And Momir says: "I still don't know what the precise situation is, what happened just now is a new thing." And Neso says: "Well, who ... let me tell you ..." And then there's something that's not understood, and then Neso says: "... well, we should take that left part and enough, damn it." And Momo says: "Well, I don't know ... we can't over the phone I'd like to -- this when I see you." And Neso says: "All right." And Momo says: "Mladic said many things, I don't know if he'll realise any of it ..." Now, these areas that are discussed here, Ilidza, Hrasnica, and Sokolovic Kolonija, those are all on the left bank of the Miljacka; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Sokolovic Kolonija, Ilidza, are both far away from Vraca, at least a dozen kilometres. So I didn't know what was going on there. I never went there to see what was happening. That was far. No Sarajevo municipality, Novi Grad municipality, and only then in Ilidza -- it must be over ten -- up to 15 kilometres from Grbavica to Ilidza and to the settlements you mentioned, Hrasnica which is below Igman and Sokolovic Kolonija which is an integral part of Hrasnica. The last two are close to each other. So I did not have an insight into what was going on there. And again I repeat about the voices that we hear in this conversation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to Ilidza only a few times in a round about ways because I had a lot of relatives there. I wanted to see whether they were alive. I had to go via Vogosca because the road was not passable, the normal, the usual road, was not passable --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sir, the question was simply whether Sokolovic Kolonija, Ilidza, and Hrasnica are on the left bank of the Miljacka and your answer and your geographic description, it appears that you can confirm that that's true. Now, when Momo Garic says that these neighbourhoods, Hrasnica -- not Ilidza, but Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija are pretty flattened or pretty damaged, that's a reference to shelling damage in those neighbourhoods; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: I repeat, how should I have known about the territory so far from Novo Sarajevo? And if that was the case, it was not done from the region where I was. That was some 10 to 15 kilometres away from there. But I cannot believe that Sokolovic Kolonija was shelled so heavily or Hrasnica for that matter. When I joined the ministry in mid-1992 according to the stories of the witnesses who came down, I wouldn't say that there was so much shelling except that there was shelling on the observed military targets. I can't believe that it was as flattened as it is implied in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija, those are both predominantly Muslim neighbourhoods or they were at the time in the municipality of Ilidza; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija are part of the municipality of Ilidza. That was the case before the war. That's how the territory had been divided. I think the inhabitants were mainly Muslims, but there were some Croats. But there were quite a few Serbs too. I don't know whether half of the inhabitants were Serbs. In Sokolovic Kolonija I had quite a few relatives, my sister, children. In certain parts of Sokolovic Kolonija built after the Olympics, there were quite a lot of Serbs. I don't know how many exactly. That was also the case in Hrasnica, not that many Serbs there and not many Croats, mainly Muslims, but there were some Serbs. But in Sokolovic Kolonija there were quite a few Serbs because Famos was in Sokolovic Kolonija and I know that many people in Famos solved accommodation issues and that there were quite a few Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P5963, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, Your Excellencies. I would like to ask the witness, since we don't have much time and I can't put leading questions, I'd like to ask the witness to answer briefly, yes and no, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you familiar with the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self Protection?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the structure of the Territorial Defence? Which units and which companies had Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: They had area and manoeuvre units. They had units in local communes and in enterprises. Enterprises had TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the president of the council for people's defence in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: In the municipality, in the Novo Sarajevo municipality? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In all municipalities, who was the president of the council for National Defence, was it the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he in command or was he not a commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't have the duties of commander. When the Crisis Staffs were established, their role was to overcome the situation, the tragedy, to deal with that. They would assemble and issue guide-lines when the executive committee in the Municipal Assembly couldn't convene the executive committee and the municipality. That is the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to make pauses but I'm hurrying. Did the chief of the section for National Defence in the municipality play the role of the commander? Did he have such duties?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: At the time it was called the secretary for National Defence in the municipality and he didn't have the function of a commander. Such person only had an advisory role and would issue instructions and guide-lines which had to do with mobilisation and improving the situation. But he didn't have the post of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the head of the Territorial Defence in the municipality, was he a commander? Did he have such a role to play?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: The head of the Territorial Defence up until the beginning of the war was a commander. He led and commanded TO units. When the war broke out, as I've been saying all day long, no TO commanders were appointed. There were prominent, respected individuals, who had reserve ranks and they fought for their people. But up until the war, the commander of the Territorial Defence staff was in charge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at P1124.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for it to appear on the screen, Mr. Garic, did the TO at its various levels have weapons warehouses?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Area units, units in local communes, had warehouses, enterprises; in Novo Sarajevo municipality, for example, prominent enterprises, Bristol hotel, the transport, school, Energoinvest, Sipad, and so on and so forth. There are many such enterprises or companies. Up until the beginning of the war these were prominent companies and made significant profit and they were in a position to buy weapons for their units. They had ammunition or weapons warehouses on their premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just verify whether this conversation was on the 23rd of April, 1992, between Momcilo Mandic and Tomislav Kovac? Just have a look at the date on the top?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of April, Momcilo Mandic, also known as Momo, and Tomislav Kovac, also known as Tomo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the date, the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at page 3 in the English version and page 4 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of duties these two performed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Tomislav Kovac before the war was a police commander in Novi Grad municipality. I think that for a certain period of time he was the minister of the interior when the Republika Srpska was formed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down. In the English version it's fine, but can we scroll down or scroll up in the Serbian version. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says Vojkovici and Lukavica should be told to fire on Sokolovic Kolonija if they attack us. They mention Vraca and the fact that an attack is expected. And it also says that they will fire only if attacked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that Kovac says we are constantly defending ourselves on Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, not only on Ilidza, but Ilidza and the area I was in, Tilava, Lukavica, Vraca, Kovacevici, Gornji Trebevic, it wasn't just Ilidza. And then on the other side on all the fronts of the Sarajevo battle-field defence had been organised. If there had been an attack, it would have been known. The lines would have been moved. But we had the status quo so this was a standard type of defence and sometimes the tactical position was improved, but this wasn't that important, so it was a matter of defence exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to have a look at the penultimate passage in Serbian. Mandic says: "I don't know these Territorial Defence members from Novo Sarajevo, well, fuck them. I don't know who is in command of them or what they're going to do ...," and so on and so forth. So the minister, or rather, the deputy minister of the interior says that he doesn't know who is in command of the Novo Sarajevo Territorial Defence members?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I've been claiming in the course of my testimony here. There was no system of subordination. There were no appointments. Yet again I'm saying that these were prominent and respected Serbs. Among them there were quite a few reserve officers and junior officers and there were also locals who were holding the line of defence in order to protect themselves and their homes because they had lived there for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the majority population in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: In Novo Sarajevo the population is mainly Serbian. If you take into consideration Gornji and Donji Pofalici, the left bank of the Miljacka river, the inhabitants are mainly Serbian but also concerns Velasici [phoen], Tilava, Miljevici, Vraca, Kovacici, many Serbian inhabitants. At the elections in the 1990s the Serbian side was victorious, the majority were Serbs, over 50 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure how that last question arose from the cross-examination. In any event, I will need to ask one question in re-cross-examination in light of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean now at the end of the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll now see what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garic, what was the majority population in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Serbian, of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Grbavica ever under the control of the ABiH? If we don't take into account infiltrations of the Green Berets, did you take back Grbavica from someone - I'm referring to the Serbs - or did you just place it under your control?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: No, the Muslim paramilitary formations never took Grbavica. They only infiltrated the area, they would beat the people, loot the people's property. But as for them ever holding that territory, no, they never held that stretch of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Garic, did the executive committee ask the head of the Territorial Defence of the military sector early on whether they would implement a decision or did they have to implement a decision on the basis of their duties?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know there was always an agreement that would be reached. Certain issues would be discussed. There weren't any real disputes or misunderstandings, so there were no real problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as that is concerned, do you see a difference between the Crisis Staff and the executive committee, or rather, the municipal authorities and who, in fact, was a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR GARIC
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff was composed of people who took care about defence, about the police, about all such matters when there was a conflict. They took care to feed the population, to provide accommodation for refugees. They were responsible for dealing with the media, for dealing with the population of other ethnicities. So this was what they had to organise when the system was breaking up. For example, Bosnia-Herzegovina used to be a rule-governed state. When the war started it was necessary for a certain period of time to pass, but things were dealt with successfully and in an organised manner and they managed to prevent tragedy from occurring, although there were certain individuals who came to harm, but that wasn't really frequently the case in the area where I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, these questions about the executive committee and the Crisis Staff. They don't arise from the cross-examination. This is not proper re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree. Mr. Karadzic, I see the time, do you have more to -- for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Perhaps just another question, but this all arises from the questions about the Crisis Staff because the Crisis Staff is nothing other than a municipal authority. You're not asked whether you want to be part of it or not. If you're part of the municipal authorities, you have to be a member of the Crisis Staff. So my question was whether he was present at the sessions that were held. Well, the authorities were municipal authorities. They wouldn't ask him whether he wanted to be present. If a task was assigned to him, he was obliged to carry out that task --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is totally inappropriate giving evidence by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not only leading, but coaching the witness. Do you have further questions? Otherwise, that being the case, we need to adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who fed and provided logistical support for the units in Republika Srpska in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, this does not arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does, Your Excellencies. It does. If municipal authorities refer to meetings -- if they're called to meetings, in fact, it's not in order to act as an authority in command but to provide food. The municipality had to feed the army. The authorities were municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not -- I have to go back, but even if it arises from the cross-examination, you are leading the witness. That's totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the question was asked about why the municipal authorities responded to military summonses and went to meetings. I asked about the role it played when it came to logistics for the army because it was suggested that the municipality had a command role to play. If this hadn't been challenged, I wouldn't have put a leading question because the fact that this arises was challenged. Of course it arises from what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That cannot be a reason for you to put a leading question, absolutely. Given the time we'll adjourn for today. We'll continue tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of November, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
